utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the locations where I think anti-aircraft weapons are drawn, in that territory, they were indeed located, and only the mortar should be drawn below what is indicated here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were questioned as to towards which targets your weapons fired on 6th of December, 1991, you said that you directed fire also at the cable-car, and you said Srdj and you used the word "cable-car." Now, when you said the word -- used the term "cable-car," which position are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cable-car emerges, if we look from the sea, to the right of Srdj, to the terrace, where part of JNA troops later emerged, and some paramilitary forces. And that's why I used this term "cable-car." We could also add --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. Is that the same position, the cable-car position where the anti-aircraft weapons positioned to the north of the Old Town were supposed to have been?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The cable-car comes out of the Srdj fortress, whereas the firing position of the anti-aircraft weapon is at the starting point of the cable-car which goes to Srdj, which is to the north or to the north-east, 120 metres away from the Old Town. That is the firing position of the anti-aircraft weapon. Whereas we were shooting at the ending point of the cable-car, which is east of the Srdj fortress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which also indicates that at that position, the cable-car position, there were JNA troops, and that's why your forces were firing at these positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We got a report from the Srdj fortress that at the ending point of the cable-car and at the terrace, JNA troops had emerged and that we should open fire, targeting that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were questioned as to whether a ZIS cannon could be used as an anti-armour weapon and you said it could be used as an anti-armour weapon as well as an anti-personnel weapon. Is a ZIS cannon a direct-fire weapon or an indirect-fire weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ZIS cannon is a direct-fire weapon. It could not be used as an anti-tank weapon if the trajectory had an elevation. That means that you use direct fire to shoot at a target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you use the ZIS cannon and fire at Zarkovica, you have a direct line of sight to Zarkovica and you can observe the fire impacting on Zarkovica from the position of the ZIS cannon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is no issue about the projectile, the trajectory or the projectile going over the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please indicate -- use the other map, sir, which is much clearer. Could you generally take your pointer cross from the ZIS cannon position at Gospino Polje to Zarkovica and show the part of the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as such, sir, does the part of the trajectory go over the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in my view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would you say is the distance from the wall of the Old Town, the northern side, to the part of the trajectory, according to the scale of this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. I would kindly ask, since we are left without a trace of something that was very obvious to all of us here, I would kindly ask my learned friend to ask the witness to draw a line, so then, when we have a line across the map, we will be able to see whether it goes across the Old Town or not. In this way, we have seen nothing. And it is obvious that the northern part of the Old Town is encompassed and is located below the trajectory. So I would like to have this drawn in. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I would not want to do that, for the simple reason this map has already been subject to markings and we have already reproduced numbers of maps. And perhaps the Defence, if they wish to do that, could possibly do it with the Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't need, I think, to bother about all those possibilities, as long as the firing point is clear. Zarkovica itself is clearly located, and anybody looking at the two can decide whether or not the trajectory goes over a part of the Old Town or not. So just make sure that the firing point is clear, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we can all do the rest after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, could you please, very clearly, point out to the Trial Chamber where exactly the firing point of the ZIS cannon at Gospino Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Polje is.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you now, please, point out where Zarkovica is.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you just indicated that -- no. I withdraw that, Your Honour. Could direct-fire weapons be used without sights, Mr. Negodic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. That's what was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain as briefly as possible as to how direct-fire weapons could be used without sights, in order that firing errors would not occur.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At such small distances, the man who manned the cannon shot through the barrel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the person who operates the weapon can see the target clearly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can he also observe the impact of fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can mortars or indirect-fire weapons be used without sights?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the period 1st October 1991 to 31st December 1991, were any indirect-fire weapons which were there within your force used without sights?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One optical sight was combined -- was used for several mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what a sighting equipment looks like in terms of size.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The size of a fist, maybe two fists, or a palm of a hand, depending on the weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is it used to fix the coordinates, firing coordinates? Can you please describe the procedure as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You measure the distance from the target, using a map, and you add the elevation, above or below, and then you detract from the distance the altitude of the firing position in relation to the target. You use the angle-measuring device and you calculate the angle on the sights on the appropriate devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain us in detail as to how you dealt with the inadequacy of sighting equipment for weapons? How was it moved and how did you ensure that the accuracy in firing was not affected by the movement of sighting equipment? When you said that sighting equipment was moved from weapon to weapon, how was it used? Did you not need a sighting equipment at a weapon constantly? Could you explain this, please, in detail perhaps.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately one optical sight was used for two weapons, if you are satisfied with that answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but when one weapon -- the sighting equipment is used with regard to one weapon, can you say how it's used, as in once you fix the coordinates, does the weapon stay in place and you do not need the sighting equipment to continue with the firing with regard to the same target continuously, or how is it used? Could you please bear in mind that we are laypersons and therefore you have to give us an idea as to how it was used.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, in order to set an objective, I have to point out that it cannot be a target that is say 50-square metres. We were targeting areas, and then this is how we operated: We only engaged a specific target, like the observation post of Zarkovica. You have to see how effective each mortar can be, and you need to have a sight for that. However, for several mortars that targeted only the area around Srdj, towards Bosanka and Strincjera, it is not necessary for them to be that precise, so they did not require sighting equipment non-stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be correct to say that once you use sighting equipment and fixed the firing coordinates of a weapon, unless the direction of fire needs to be changed with regard to that weapon, you don't need to resort to that sighting equipment again? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we look at a given point in time, or rather, a given period, we can see whether there were any changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So once the equipment is used and the target -- the weapon is directed towards the particular target, you could move the sight equipment to another weapon and you don't need the sight equipment for that original weapon unless you need to change the direction of fire. Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that already in relation to the previous question, the witness said what he had to say about a sight that is mounted and that is used subsequently, and I think that this now is a leading question, dealing with it yet again, or rather, putting the answer into the question that is being put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think on balance, Mr. Rodic, what counsel is attempting to do is to summarise what had gone before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But, really, it's labouring the point. We could move on, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you just respond, though, to my question, Mr. Negodic, before I move on, with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If one would be used, then it would be transferred to the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did you have forward observers for your mortar and artillery positions in addition to yourself observing the fire missions and issuing directions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For combat positions with two mortars, they do not have a visible target in that sense. So I was the observer from the firing positions of two ZIS cannons and one rocket launcher. They can see the target for themselves from their own position, and they can correct their own fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my point is: For -- in direct-fire weapons, where, for instance, in the case of mortars, where they could not see the targets, were forward observers utilised to observe fire and correct the firing of the particular weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam. I was the only one who could have been in that particular function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were you in a position, then, to observe fire of all your heavy weapons positions and to correct the firing? Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, that was for two firing positions. A 120-millimetre shell was supposed to fall 200 metres left of Srdj, then I would give a correction of 200 metres, and from their firing position it is no longer on the right-hand side like it is my right-hand side. On the map, they make corrections, and for them, it would be, let's put it that way, 200 metres more. So when I gave a correction to the first mortar, then they continued to deal with it in that way, namely, that they introduced the corrections by dealing with the elevation and the direction on the sighting equipment. The mortars are one next to the other. In our case, the required military set-up was not observed, because the terrain would not allow it either. So the distance between the mortars was not as prescribed usually. That can be reflected in terms of 20 or 30 metres in the area. Since we were targeting areas, that was negligible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said you had to observe fire and correct fire with regard to two positions. What are those positions, please? Could you name them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The firing position of mortars from auto camp Solitudo and the firing position for mortars by the SDK building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other weapons that were active on 6 December 1991, according to what you indicated so far, were all direct-fire weapons, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this context, sir, who directed the fire mission, or who acted as the observer and the person who corrected the fire during that 40 minutes time when you were absent from the position? That's the time when Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you drove to the hospital. I think you did indicate a name. Could you just say as to who replaced you during this period.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That job was taken over by the command, by Mirko Katanic, in the following way: They established direct contact with Fort Srdj and the crew from Fort Srdj had the role of defender but that of observer at the same time in order to be able to guide fire from Srdj to headquarters and then to the firing position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to discuss afterwards with this person, with Mirko Katanic, as to what had transpired during these 40 minutes that you were absent? Do you know if during this 40 minutes whether there had been any firing errors from -- on the part of your forces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, and then I took over again. There were no indications of any mistake having been made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You were questioned as to the movement of mortars in the course of firing. Isn't there something called a base plate fixed to the end of the mortar weapon? And could you, in terms of the base plate, describe to the Trial Chamber how a weapon settles into the ground with firing and we should avoid movement of the weapon in the course of firing. And bear in mind, sir, that we are laypersons, so could you just describe the process.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A mortar is dug into the ground, depending on the surface involved, using a particular angle. However, if a mortar is placed properly, after several firings from a mortar, if the surface is soft, then it acts partly as a shock absorber and partly not. That is why I said a while ago that after a few shells are fired, the sights have to be used again and the base plate has to be lifted so that this could be adjusted accordingly. So once a mortar is placed on the ground, it doesn't mean that the mortar will stay in place. After a few rounds are fired, it slowly sinks into the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that way, doesn't the base plate dig into the ground and doesn't the weapon get settled in position after firing several rounds?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is dug into the ground at a particular angle so that the surface would play a proper role. However, the more rounds are fired, the mortar itself pushes the earth, and especially if the earth is soft or moist, after a few shells are fired, the mortar starts sinking in. So again, the sights have to be used for making a correction and the mortar has to be placed properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were questioned about a detachment of armed boats in the Dubrovnik defence. With what weapons were these boats armed? First and foremost, would you indicate as to how many such boats were there.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know details involving ammunition supplies for the artillery. As for speedboats, there were some weapons on them, but I cannot explain which kind. I know that they called it the detachment of armed boats. In my opinion, it wasn't really the Croatian army; it was volunteers. Now, what they called it and who gave approval for that is something that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the type of boat that was used? You indicated speedboats. Is that all you had or were there other types of vessels involved?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just speedboats, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about approximately how many were used?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they deployed on 6 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the details. My opinion is that they were in the bay of the island of Kolocep. This bay is on the western side of the island.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as at 6 December 1991, wasn't there a full maritime and also -- I'm sorry, full maritime blockade established by the JNA around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a complete blockade from the sea in place as at 6 December 1991, a blockade established by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already stated, all ships of the Yugoslav navy were in the area between Cavtat and Kupari. That is the bay of Zupa, Zupska Uvala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there JNA vessels around Dubrovnik as at 6 December 1991? And I'm not asking whether they were firing, I'm asking: Was there a presence of JNA vessels around Dubrovnik to ensure that there was no breach of the blockade? I'm not asking about vessels firing, but presence of vessels.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said just now, that is immediately nearby, perhaps a kilometre from the road leading from Dubac to Dubrovnik. But they were not in front of Lapad or something like that, if that's what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your speedboats free to move about without being detected by the JNA vessels? And I'm specifically referring to 6 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, they were anchored where I said. As far as I know, there weren't any actions going on, although amongst ourselves we were sort of laughing about the expression they had coined, this detachment of armed boats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain why you found it funny. As briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because there was perhaps a light machine-gun on it or something like that, and what can that do to a war ship? It was along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that why, when I asked you in examination-in-chief, as to whether the Dubrovnik defence had a naval force, you responded in the negative? Is it because of the inadequacy of this alleged force, naval force, that you say that you -- that the Dubrovnik defence force did not have a naval force?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, meaning that part of the navy, with a command post in the hotel of Komodor, it only secured a very narrow belt by the coastline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You were questioned with regard to confrontation lines of the Croatian forces, and at one point a question was put to you to this effect, whether a new defence line was set up between Orsula - and pardon my pronunciation - Srdj Hill, Nuncijata, Sustjepan and along the coastline from Babin Kuk to -- through the Old Town -- not through, to the Old Town. Now, was there ever a defence line - and I mean in terms of infantry lines or confrontation lines - by the Old Town, in close proximity to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: West of the Old Town, there is an area called Gradac. As far as I know, there was a group there of 10 or 15 infantrymen which would prevent entry into a very small harbour which is here on the map, where there's a church. So that is to the west of the Old Town. You can see the marking for a church and a beach. And it's only that group of men that was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the distance to that position from the walls of the Old Town on the western side?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two hundred fifty metres, three hundred, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the ZIS cannons that your forces had, they were 76 millimetre, isn't it? And I ask that because in the record at certain times it has gone down as 66 millimetre. You had only 76-millimetre ZIS cannons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 76.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were only two positions, as at 6 December 1991, containing ZIS cannons, which were at Mala Petka and Gospino Polje?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were questioned about an alleged clash between a unit of military police on 6 December 1991, and you said that you had in fact heard about it afterwards. Did you have any information that in the course of this alleged clash, there were any -- as a result of it, any persons were killed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no. It was a clash that was due to the influence of alcohol only, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what type of a clash was this? Was it a very major type of clash with firing of weapons, heavy weapons, or was it just a minor quarrel between soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it had to be characterised very precisely, and I already have said that it was under the influence of alcohol, I think that this answer will do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is? I'm sorry, sir. Which answer will do? Is it -- was it a minor quarrel or was it a major fight, as such?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not everybody takes drink the same way. Probably somebody, one of them, took out a pistol and fired two or three bullets, and they probably quarreled, and that's the only explanation I can give you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the course of cross-examination, at two points you -- your response has been recorded as this, and I'll read it to you: "I said during the first day when the lady was putting her questions to me, I cannot say that there were only hunting guns there." This is a reference to what was present within the Old Town. Did you mean to say: "I cannot say that there were only hunting guns there," or did you mean to say: "I can say that there were only hunting guns there"? Which of these is correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wished to say was that I think that only hunting guns or pistols, so personal weapons, were in town. There weren't any artillery pieces, either on the walls or within the Old Town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And also in the same vein, you go on to say, I will quote it to you verbatim: "As far as I know, no, because the explicit order issued to all commanders was to convey to the soldiers not only for them to remain within the Old Town but that at all costs they should avoid being even close to it." Did you mean to say that the order was not to remain within the Old Town? Is that what you meant to say? Because it has been recorded as "not only for them to remain within the Old Town." Which of these is correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was sent to the commanders to convey to their soldiers that not a single person had any business whatsoever within the Old Town. Are you satisfied with this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not everything was interpreted, everything that should be interpreted. He said that not a single uniformed person had any business whatsoever within the Old Town. The word "uniformed" is missing from the transcript, so could it please be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, considering that you said that during this time, most of your soldiers did not have uniforms, what orders had you received with regard to soldiers who were not in uniform being present within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the command, since we had professional people, professional officers, of course what they wrote in their orders was persons in uniform, and then it was up to us to convey to each and every unit commander how to regulate this, namely, that each and every one of them should know that this pertained to their entire crews, regardless of whether they were wearing uniforms or not. Perhaps I should repeat this. A professional soldier of the former Yugoslavia could not write in an order that civilians in civilian clothes would not be allowed to enter the Old Town. So I assume that that is the explanation that should be given. Perhaps I should just add something else, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we have reached the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can have another five minutes, if you need it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I do need perhaps 15 minutes. I wonder whether I could seek Your Honours' indulgence, perhaps, during the next session, to take another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll carry on for a little while now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, I'm under time constraints, so I'd really appreciate it if you could respond as briefly as possible where possible, sir. You stated that on 6 December, your fire was concentrated on Srdj, the fortress and the slopes and Zarkovica. Now, clearly by your evidence Croat units were positioned at the fortress at Srdj. So could you explain very briefly as to the objective of the fire directed at Srdj. How did you eliminate any possibility of your own forces positioned at Srdj not being affected by this fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already told you, madam, and as I have told the gentleman from the Defence too, it is a fortress built by Napoleon and it is solidly built. I said we were targeting the Srdj fortress and the area around it, and the eastern part of the cable-car, that is, the terrace. When the members of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. As I was saying, when we're talking specifically about Fort Srdj, I mean the eastern part of the Fort Srdj, which is connected with the cable-car. And of course, we were supposed to target the fortress itself, namely, its eastern part. Any overshoots, any projectiles that would not hit the fortress, would fall in the area where the infantry was. And even if we overshot across the fortress, we would still be hitting the area where the infantry was advancing towards us. I hope this answer is sufficient. If you need additional explanation, I'll provide it. The area from the Bosanka --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as such, what you were targeting on Srdj were approaching units of the JNA, the units that were approaching the Srdj fort?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of cross-examination, you made a correction to your testimony by stating that on 6 December 1991, the naval forces of the JNA did not attack. Now, in the course of my questioning to you in examination-in-chief, you spoke of certain details of JNA vessels firing. Could you just indicate the time frame you are referring to then. What was the attack you were talking about then? Since it was not 6 December 1991, when was that attack carried out, the attack you described in the course of examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was almost on a daily basis that shelling occurred. I would say that in the month of November, it was the 9th, 10th, 11th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the reference to firing from naval vessels in your statement also refers to this time frame, then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I corrected myself and I said that it was not the case on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know at which targets the Maljutka near President Hotel in Lapad fired on 6 December 1991, since you indicated that there were no naval forces firing at you from the JNA side on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was not in operation that day. It was meant to act against ships and it had no target at the time. And there were no adequate targets for that type of weapon from that firing position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me one more thing. I'm not feeling very well health-wise, and I am asking you kindly to speed this up, or I don't know how to put it. I'm not feeling very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would it help if we had a break now, Mr. Negodic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it would. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break now and resume, and you can have another five minutes after we resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown document D77, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, are you feeling all right now? Are you in a position to perhaps answer a few more questions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown this document by the Defence. Could you indicate the date of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19th December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know as to when the equipment, the ammunition or weapons that I indicated there, were delivered to the -- to your forces? And you don't have to give an exact date. Was it after 6 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Items such cannon, rocket weapon Pauk 9211, mortars, et cetera, is the situation up to the 6th of December, and what is indicated here is 120 grenades. That was brought after the 6th, that is, between the 6th and the 19th. I would not be able to tell you more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the 6th of December, 1991, did your forces receive additional ammunition and equipment? And I'm referring to the period after the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the contents of this document refers to a situation which was after 6 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it is indicated here, the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you indicated that your positions at Bogisica Park and Lazareti fired only once in November 1991 and that the position at Ivo Vojnovic Street in Gospino Polje fired only on 6 December 1991. My question to you is, sir: Now, did the fact that your forces were subject to limitation of ammunition have any impact on the number of times particular firing positions were active?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam. The shortage of ammunition and the impossibility of regular resupply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were questioned about certain hotels in Dubrovnik and in the wider area of Dubrovnik providing food to the soldiers of the Dubrovnik defence force, and you were shown, in fact, two documents, D75 and D76. My question to you is: Were there any hotels within the Old Town of Dubrovnik, within the Old Town, which had any form of military activity or which provided any military support to the Dubrovnik defence force within the period 1st October 1991 to 31st December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about several hotels by name, for example, Neptun, Stadion, President, Adriatic, Komodor, and some other hotels. Now, where were these hotels located? You don't have to give the exact positions. Was it in the wider area of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the area of Lapad. Only Stadion Hotel is in the area of Gruz. These hotels indicated here represent only a part of all hotels located in that territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the hotel which was closest to the Old Town which provided food to the forces of the Dubrovnik defence force? I'm saying what was the hotel which was closest to the Old Town in terms of proximity?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these hotels are far from the Old Town. The closest one to Gruz is the Stadion Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how far is it in terms of kilometres from the walls of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A kilometre and a half, approximately. I cannot say precisely. I mean as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You said that you had heard from the police that there were sling guns and shotguns within the Old Town. And when you said sling guns and shotguns, the presence thereof, was it in terms of a substantial quantity or were you talking about individuals having their individual weapons within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about the number, but they were held by civilians, refugees from Konavle and other places, who were accommodated, put up, in the Old Town. I suppose that there were some shotguns also in hotels, where refugees were put up, again from the locations I indicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're talking about is the individual weapons belonging to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in conclusion: Who was in charge of the artillery and mortar sector -- I'm sorry. I rephrase it. You said in evidence that you were in charge of the artillery and mortar sector of the Dubrovnik defence force for the period 1st October 1991 through December 1991. Now, my question was: In such circumstances, were you in a position to know exactly what weapons your force, the Dubrovnik defence force, had during this period in terms of artillery and mortars?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes the re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Negodic, you'll be pleased to know that that brings to an end the need for you to be here. Thank you very much for coming and for the time that you've spent with us and the assistance you have given us. And you are now free to return to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is, and I'd just like to inquire of the usher if the next witness is in fact ready to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Wait a moment for the usher to return.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will go and check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Mr. Davorin Rudolf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rudolf. Would you be kind enough to take the affirmation on the card that is handed to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rudolf.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please, for the record, give your entire name, your date of birth, your place of birth, and your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rudolf. Could you give, please, a bit of your educational background, your higher education, that is, professional degrees, if any.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I graduated from the law school. I have a Ph.D. in law and I specialised in international law at Princeton and New York universities in the United States. Is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rudolf. Are you currently still working?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: No, not professionally. But I do lecture at the university to postgraduate studies, the subject being international relations, but I am not a full-time lecturer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, when and what your particular task or obligation, rank was and where you served.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: In 1957 and 1958, I graduated from the school for reserve officers, the quartermaster's service, and my latest rank in the Yugoslav People's Army was junior lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you serve in the course of your time in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: The first six months I served in Sarajevo, and another six months in Sinj, which is a small place near Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of the year 1991, the entire year, did you belong to any political party?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: No, not in 1991. I was not a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the end of 1991, had you ever become a member of a party? If so, what party; and for how long did you remain, if you left it?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: From 1993 to 1999, I was a member of the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your career, have you authored any works that are in the public domain?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: In the public domain, that is, disregarding my professional papers, I wrote a book about the 1991 war, titled "The War We Did Not Want." Croatia, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you written other works concerning your professional interests?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote a number of books dealing with the permanent neutrality of Austria and Switzerland, I also wrote a textbook about international maritime law, an encyclopedic dictionary of international maritime law, another book about the economic zone, and I also wrote a book titled "Epicontinental Belt," and of course a number of specialist articles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is maritime law an area of particular interest or perhaps specialisation?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I specialised in international law, and within international law, there is one segment called the international law of the sea, which was a natural choice for me because I live on the coast, in the town of Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever served in a cabinet position for the government of Croatia, whether during socialist times or subsequently?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: In 1990, in July 1990, I became a minister in the Croatian government, minister for maritime affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you hold that ministry?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I held that post until August 1992, and in the meantime, for a while, in 1991, I held the portfolio of minister of foreign affairs at the same time when I was minister for maritime affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hold the position of minister of maritime affairs during the time period 1 October -- or let us make it 1 September 1991 through 31 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the Croatian government in your ministry position, did you or were you asked by your government to take part in various aspects of negotiations concerning the conflict in Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. On behalf of the Croatian government, I negotiated and signed an agreement with General Cad in Rijeka on the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from that area, and of course a cessation of all combat activities, and that agreement pertained to the area from the Slovenian border to the town of Crkvenica. In the night between the 8th and 9th November, 1991, that agreement was signed. Later, in Zitnic, a small place near Knin, I negotiated and signed another agreement with General Vukovic, who was at that time the JNA general for that area, and that concerned the withdrawal and cessation of hostilities from Crkvenica to the place called Ploce, in the valley of the Neretva River. And later, in Cavtat, together with another two ministers in the Croatian government, I signed another agreement, on the 7th December 1991, with General Jokic. That is, we represented --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say General Jokic? Was that the --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I'm sorry, he was Admiral Jokic. He was actually vice admiral. And we signed that agreement with Vice Admiral Jokic, covering the area from Metkovici to the Montenegro border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll return to the 7 of December agreement shortly. Where were you based that you were tasked by your government to handle all these various negotiations with officers? And can you confirm -- I'm sorry. I want to make sure -- you have confirmed that the generals Cad and Vukovic were JNA generals. Two questions there. Where were you based? And I'm just confirming that your negotiations were with JNA senior officers.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Regarding the first two agreements, I was based in Zagreb, and from there I travelled to Rijeka, and later to Zitnic, twice. Zitnic was then under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army. We first travelled to Split, and from there to Zitnic. I went to Zitnic twice. And regarding the third agreement signed with Admiral Jokic, I was based in the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the negotiations that you were involved in and have just discussed also involve areas which were under a naval blockade?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. This third agreement that we concluded in Cavtat for the area of Dubrovnik, it included the area around the town of Dubrovnik that was under a naval blockade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the other areas that you were involved in at any time also under a -- if they were areas where appropriately naval blockades might apply, were they under blockade?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. The Yugoslav People's Army had placed a blockade on the entire sea, on the entire coastline of the Republic of Croatia. For example, when I went to Dubrovnik, that area in front of the town of Rijeka was also under a blockade. There was a war ship off the coast. However, later, the blockades were lifted, but the blockade for the town of Dubrovnik remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of the 1st of December, was Dubrovnik the only port that remained under naval blockade?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time period of, let's say, 1 October through 31 December, what had happened in Vukovar? I'm sorry. Let me put the year in. Of course 1991. When I refer, it's 1991, unless I otherwise state.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Vukovar was under siege and under constant attack from the Yugoslav People's Army. For -- only just before we came to Dubrovnik, Vukovar had fallen. That is the vocabulary we used. And there were terrible casualties and destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to give an estimate of the percentage of Croatian territory which had been, let's say up to the time we're talking about, under occupation?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Approximately 27 per cent, around 27 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a point in time where the government of Croatia, as part of a larger international effort, saw the need to undertake the peaceful withdrawal of the JNA from its territory?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I'm talking from my own personal experience now. The government of Croatia made efforts all the time to prevent and stop the war. Unfortunately, this is neglected by the public, but I'll give you an example. In mid-1991, the Croatian government offered an official proposal to have a type of confederation, an alliance of sovereign states. At that time, I was minister of foreign affairs and, if you will, I was the one who drafted the document. I can just tell you that I had contacts with all the republics at that time, and we also sent this draft to the European Community, nowadays the European Union, in Brussels. And then also to all the main capitals, that is to say in the United States of America and all other centres of power. And with the representatives of all the republics, including Montenegro, we agreed, in principle, that such an agreement would be useful and it could have prevented any further warfare in Yugoslavia. It is only in Belgrade that this proposal was not accepted. Of course, these agreements were made after agreements in principle were reached at international conferences. I'm referring to a particular one in Geneva, namely, to have the JNA withdraw from the territory of Croatia. If I remember correctly, this was the 23rd of October, 1991. That's when this agreement was reached. But perhaps we could double-check the exact date at this point in time. This had to do with the withdrawal of the JNA from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was looking to ask you about the end of November and whether there were, in fact, international agreements, conferences, that were dealing with this issue, particularly out of Geneva.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. In Geneva and right here in The Hague. In the preamble of this agreement that we signed in Cavtat, there is reference to an agreement of this nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you categorise how high a priority the arrangement, the negotiation of the peaceful withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of Croatia was for the Croatian government, and particularly by the end of November.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Of course this was very important for the Croatian government. The priority of Croatia at that time was certainly to bring the war to an end, to stop the war, to stop the destruction, the casualties. I can tell you that we in the government also thought about how to stop major destruction in the towns of Croatia. So one of the motives for the agreements related to Rijeka and Split and Dubrovnik later was to stop destruction in major Croatian towns and cities. Of course throughout Croatia, but you can imagine what Croatia would have looked like if the big cities were destroyed. Even Zagreb, a European metropolis, had been shelled from the occupied territories near Knin, to the north of Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of negotiations on a local level, or perhaps a series of negotiations on a local level in the Dubrovnik area that had been taking place since, let us say, beginning of October through, let us say, late November?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. Negotiations were conducted with local representatives, of course, between the representatives of the JNA and the representatives of the town of Dubrovnik. And I even know that there were negotiators from the town of Dubrovnik and that one of them was Mr. Obuljen. However, regrettably, these agreements were not honoured. One of the reasons that led us to finally stop these wars and destruction was to have agreements concluded between the government of Croatia and the top leadership of the Yugoslav People's Army, the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the government of Croatia, are you talking about a level higher than local negotiators?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I'm talking about the highest level. The government of Croatia, to my mind, is the highest level. And on the other side, it is the General Staff, or rather, the supreme command of the armed forces, that is to say, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you and the other ministers you referred to earlier part of that highest level of the Croatian government involved in negotiations in December about Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... names of your two colleagues, the other ministers who also were involved, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Mr. Petar Kriste, his nickname is Pero, who was minister of trade at the time [Realtime transcript omitted the words "who was minister of trade at the time], and Ivan Cifric, who was minister of the environment and housing in the government of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would ask for a moment. Did you work with monitors from the European Community Monitoring Mission in the course of your work in all areas? Not just Dubrovnik, but generally in the course of working with the government of Croatia to try to orchestrate the withdrawal of the JNA, among other matters?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The transcript only says Mr. Petar Kriste but it doesn't say that he was minister of trade. So could that please be corrected. So yes, we were in contact with the European Community in Jakar [phoen], Zitnic, and Dubrovnik. We were in touch with them in Dubrovnik also when this agreement, this final agreement, was being discussed. And as a matter of fact, the representative of the European Community co-signed the agreement. I can't remember his name now. I don't know if I can pronounce his name properly. He was a Dutchman. He was the deputy of the main representative of the European Community for the entire area there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- was there a JNA officer in Zagreb who also served as a liaison officer to the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I don't know who was exactly in charge of liaising with the monitoring mission, but the liaison officer between the government and the Yugoslav People's Army was General Andrija Raseta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I have --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: We communicated with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask, please, that the document from tab 5 of your binders be provided or looked at.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For Your Honours' information, this is not a composite exhibit, the binder. It is to facilitate looking at individual items therein.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, which has already been tendered into evidence -- can I ask you, please, Mr. Rudolf, is the English okay or do you want a copy in your own language as well? I think -- are we looking -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: English version. The English version is fine. As a matter of fact, I think that the English version is sometimes better than these translations of ours into the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... what you have is from tab 5. It looks to me like it's a shorter document. I'm looking at one that has been tendered earlier. Thank you. We're just correcting that, Mr. Rudolf and Your Honours. Just to ask you to take a quick you look through it, please, and indicate whether you're familiar with the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: No. I have not seen this document until now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... content of the document I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, the content, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: However, the document, as a document, I see for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm asking you now what is contained in it. And are you familiar with -- first of all, it is dated 24 November 1991, and it makes reference to, among other things, the need to find -- in the second to the last paragraph -- practical solutions to the direct and acute problem facing cities like Vukovar, Osijek, and Dubrovnik while the blocked JNA units are leaving and The Hague Peace Conference remains suspended. Does the general situation depicted or set out in this document reflect, in your view, what the situation was when you were tasked to negotiate the Dubrovnik situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I cannot read all of this very carefully now, but I think it's about right. I would have to read it very carefully in order to give you a very accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you, if perhaps I can, in the interests of time, just direct your attention to the points which suggest that one of the considerations, at the end of the second to last paragraph is -- it says: "Either a separate agreement is reached, which in essence will give Dubrovnik a status apart, or hostilities will resume and justify the fait accompli of a breach of cease-fire and further destruction of the ancient city." Was a concern for the continued security or perhaps lack of security a motivating factor as well, if you recall your own mandate. Security in Dubrovnik, the situation, the dangers that were there, was that a concern in Zagreb as to negotiating the agreement on the --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What do you mean when you say lack of security or continued security or dangers? I mean, Dubrovnik was totally surrounded by Yugoslav People's Army units from land, and there was a naval blockade on the sea. So Dubrovnik was in an exceptionally difficult position. Of course, this caused great concern among us, if that is what you meant by security. And we made every possible effort at that time for this brutal situation to be resolved. The people of Dubrovnik were suffering: They had no electricity, they had no water, it was very cold, and there were these constant attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "attacks," Mr. Rudolf, are you -- was the government aware of the use -- the presence and use of heavy weaponry by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: My goodness, yes. It was attacked from land and sea. I think you have authentic recordings of attacks on Dubrovnik. I was minister of maritime affairs and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for clarifying that. The mandate that you got by your government to go to Dubrovnik, can you give us, please, a chronology, at least in terms of what happened first, how were you brought into this negotiation, where were you, from where did you go, how did you go? And may I first ask: Did you have contact at the federal level of the former Yugoslavia about these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: The Prime Minister of Croatia, Mr. Greguric, told me, I think on the 28th or 29th of November, that I would be going to Dubrovnik together with two ministers. And on the 29th, we received instructions in writing to travel to Dubrovnik straight away on behalf of the government. What was most important was to attain two objectives, first and foremost; to stop hostilities in the area and to have the JNA withdrawn in accordance with the agreements that we signed for the Rijeka and Split regions. We were also charged with the task of representing the government in Metkovic, on the island of Korcula, to work on resolving problems of supplies, refugees, to establish contact with the representatives of the European Community, but, of course, our most important task was to achieve a deblockade of the port of Dubrovnik, a cessation of hostilities in the area, and the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army. Immediately --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Would you -- was this, then, a comprehensive set of negotiations that would have covered cessation of hostilities when you discuss the multiple things -- set of this negotiations as a comprehensive set?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. Later on we conducted these negotiations. Actually, this was the last agreement that was supposed to resolve all these questions, from the river of Neretva all the way to the Croatian-Montenegrin border, or rather, the border between Croatia and Yugoslavia at that time. May I proceed now? Since Dubrovnik was under blockade and the talks there were supposed to be agreed upon, I cannot say exactly, but twice or three times I talked to General Raseta. He had his office at Ig Hotel [phoen] in Zagreb and we agreed straight away that negotiations should be held. I particularly insisted on having them give us safe conduct, because the question was how we could reach Dubrovnik. Also, I asked for them to vouch for our personal safety and security and that there should be no armed operations going on during the negotiations. He agreed on all of that in principle, and he told me that finally this had to be resolved at a high level, because these negotiations between local Croatian authorities and the Yugoslav People's Army were not very effective. He told me on that occasion that I would be negotiating in Dubrovnik with General Strugar. I asked to have this in writing, but he could not give me any guarantees in writing. The following day, we took a car down to Split. It was very hard to get even to Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we leave Zagreb, did you have any opportunity to reach anyone in Belgrade about this set of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Not that day. Not that day. We travelled to Split. Because it was hard even to get to Split. Part of the road near the town of Zadar was open to attacks, possible attacks from the Yugoslav People's Army, so it was very hard to go there. So we were there with three cars, and we had to go one at a time. So we reached Split the next morning. And from the office of the president of the Executive Council of the town of Split, as it was called at that time, I called the office of Admiral Brovet in Belgrade. I think that Admiral Brovet was the highest-ranking official in the Yugoslav navy. I talked to the people who worked in his office. I repeated all these things that I asked from Mr. Raseta. I reiterated these requests and I received guarantees verbally that everything would be all right, but I didn't get anything in writing. Otherwise, I live in Split, so when I came home, my wife told me that she got a telephone call from General Raseta's office - I forgot the name of the officer who made the telephone call - stating that we had guaranteed passage to Dubrovnik and personal safety. So I asked Belgrade for this kind of permission and in the evening we had talks with General Mladenic about the departure of the JNA from Split. There was a very big naval base called Lora, and also in Divulje, a small place near Split, there is another naval base, so we were discussing the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from there. Also I asked for Admiral Kandic, who was commander of the navy for the entire naval district, as it was called at the time, that he should also give me guarantees for safe conduct. Mr. Mladenic, or rather, General Mladenic, told me that Admiral Kandic's message was that we could pass through there but I never got anything in writing. The following day --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you: Were you working also at the time with representatives of the European Community Monitoring Mission, with the ECMM? Were they also part of this group, if you recall, once you were in Split? If you don't recall, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I can't be sure. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come to leave Split for Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: In the morning, we left Split on a ship of the coastal -- of the Port Authority, about 20 metres long. We were travelling to Dubrovnik, and when we came close to Dubrovnik, the captain of this vessel tried to establish contact with the Yugoslav navy and contact was established. Right in front of Dubrovnik there is a small islet called St. Andrija, and we were told from the Yugoslav warship to go around that island and there we saw an anchored war ship. We approached it, stopped by the ship, and an officer came down from the ship to our boat, made a very superficial inspection, and allowed us to go on. We arrived in Dubrovnik on the 3rd in the evening, at the Gruz port, where we were met by representatives of the town. I remember Mr. Poljanic, the man number one of Dubrovnik, was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please: When you travelled from Split to Dubrovnik -- well, first of all --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I lost the interpretation. I can't hear anything. Can we turn it up a little?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- are you familiar with the name Hvalkof, Hvalkof?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. That is -- I was not sure about my pronunciation. That is the representative of the European Community who was present when we signed this agreement, and I believe he was the deputy --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: ECMM monitors, observers, were travelling with us. I'm not sure that he was with us, but he was with us in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you got to Dubrovnik, where was your accommodation? Where were you staying?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: When we arrived in Dubrovnik, we were met, as I said, by the representatives of the town, and we were driven to Argentina Hotel, which is located to the south of the Old Town. And there is a small annex to the hotel where we were accommodated, together with the representatives of the European Community. There was a UN representative, Mr. Stephan Di Mistura, and as soon as we got there, representatives of the city authorities informed us of the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me one second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Hotel Argentina -- the location of the Hotel Argentina generally -- are you from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: No. I'm from Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the same Hotel Argentina where all the -- where the monitors and other internationals had been housed or situated during much of the conflict, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. There in that annex building there was a bar, on the right-hand there was a restaurant, and they had a separate room on the left-hand side. They were all there together with us. There was even --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is this the same hotel that is to the south-east of the Old Town? The same Argentina that is south-east of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: South-east, east, all right, yes. Maybe it's south-east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... same hotel. Thank you very much. I'd like to ask you please --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- from tab -- excuse me one second. I'll make sure I have the right tab. The last tab 40 -- sorry -- tab 17. It does not an accompanying English translation, at least not in my binder. And I apologise, I just wanted to ask you about this particular document. Are you familiar with the -- this -- the contents of this document, which is dated 28 November 1991? And it comes from the command of Dubrovnik municipality. Are you familiar with the content?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: You see, lots of these documents passed through my hand at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. When we were discussing -- in fact, when we were presented with a situation in Dubrovnik, when we were apprised of the situation, we were told at the same time that incidents like this, sniping incidents, also occurred. We were told this by representatives of Dubrovnik, Mr. Poljanic and Mr. Sikic, who was president of the Executive Board at the time, but this document, such as this one from the command of the defence of Dubrovnik, was one of the many we received while I was down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will ask at this point just to have it marked for identification, please, and I will turn to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to have interrupted the other train of thought. I just wanted to see about the types of communications, the span of communications that you had been kept abreast of. Now, when you got to the Dubrovnik area, was there generally a cease-fire in effect? Was there generally an act of hostility going on upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: You mean when we arrived there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It occurs to me that I asked for it to be marked and I did not get a number, and I apologise. 161. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Dear madam, you mean when we got down there to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: We arrived on the 4th, in the evening. And when we got out onto the coast, it was quiet. Then the mayor showed us around and explained the situation. Dubrovnik is a town behind which there is a hill called Srdj, and on top of that hill there is an old fortress. Imperijal, it's called. That's a very well-known fortress on Srdj hill. He said: There are the units of the Croatian army; and to the left and to the right, that is, to the east and west, units of the Yugoslav People's Army are located. When you get out and when you see this -- Dubrovnik is a small town, you know. The blockade was complete from land and sea, and it was a very difficult situation. When we got to the hotel, they gave us more details about the situation, and we established contact on the same day with the liaison officer, whose name was Sofronije Jeremic. He was a JNA officer. And we agreed with him to start negotiations on the next day, on the 5th of December, in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... liaison officer for which forces? Sofronije Jeremic was the liaison officer for -- I mean JNA or Croatian?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: JNA. When I say "liaison officer," he was the man with whom we were constantly in contact. I don't know if "liaison officer" is the right term. He was an officer, and I don't know his precise rank. So we agreed with him that the next day, on the 5th, in the morning, we would go to Cavtat, in the morning - Cavtat is a small place to the east of Dubrovnik- and that we would hold negotiations there with the admiral of the Yugoslav navy, Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you, please: We're going to go through some documents and so we're going to try to focus a bit. And tab 3, for Your Honours and Mr. Rudolf, looking at a document of multiple pages that we have referred to for shorthand as "the harbour master's log," but it is called -- in your language, what is the title of the document, please, that you see? The very first page of the document in the Croatian language, what is the title of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Radio log, Radio Nemik [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it indicate that the area, for example -- is there anything to indicate if it has to do with the naval or land-based communications, or what else does it say on the front, if you can read it, please? What else is written on the front of that besides Radio Nemik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: What's written here is not legible. There's something written, and below that a date indicating when the log was started, and I can see some text. In larger naval towns, there are naval radio stations. Dubrovnik had one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... turn --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: -- within the ministry for naval affairs of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "naval affairs," are you referring to maritime affairs? Is it the ministry of maritime affairs?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the maritime affairs, communications between ships and with ships, within the port authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at the next page, please, which has -- it has at the top -- it has some numbers printed it on, and the numbers are 01067001. At the bottom of that page, by the date, there is what appears to be a seal. Can you see that, a seal?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. Port Authority of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what ministry is listed on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Ministry of maritime affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the ministry over which you were minister at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are communications of your ministry, or communications that concern matters which fall under the competence or jurisdiction of your ministry, are some of those communications logged or entered into this type of document as a matter of practice or regulation?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. That is under the jurisdiction of the ministry for maritime affairs. However, you have to bear in mind that there are several such port authorities: Rijeka, Split, Dubrovnik, in all larger places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this particular document refer to the Dubrovnik local representative of the ministry of maritime affairs, what we're calling the harbour-master, as it were?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF
utterances.text: Yes. The port authority was headed by the head of the port authority, the captain, and there were other officers below him. And among other things, they had their own radio stations. Such radio stations were used when ships set off or set into a port. Communications with mainland, and between ships, and between mainland and ships, all that was carried out using these radio stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in principle, the Defence has no objection to introducing this document into evidence. However, it is incomplete. It contains only the first 10 pages, whereas the total number of pages is 196. And if my learned friend wants this tendered into evidence, then the Defence would kindly ask that the entire document be introduced. Because this also refers to another potential exhibit which we will discuss later today or perhaps tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're happy to give the entire document. We thought that what was relevant from it would be the most appropriate part to seek to introduce here.
